Did you see the shipping story this morning?
I did. The strait, which carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been closed for eleven days now.
Everyone is talking about the oil price. I am not sure it changes anything for us.
Not this month. But the plants whose parts come from Asia are already reporting delays, and a plant that is behind runs on overtime.
And overtime is your line, not mine.
It is. And the teams whose managers have been pushing them since January are the ones we lose first.
What is the outlook, then? Give me your honest one.
Volatile, which is the word people use when nobody knows. What I would watch is the overtime line in the two plants we talked about last month.

Good morning, and welcome to the weekly business briefing. Our main story is the strait that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, which has been closed to some vessels for eleven days now. The immediate effect is on shipping insurance, which has more than doubled since the beginning of the month. The knock-on effects are slower and larger. Companies whose factories depend on parts from Asia are already reporting delays of two to three weeks, and the outlook for the next quarter is described by almost every analyst as volatile. What does that mean for people who do not work in logistics? It means longer hours in the plants that are trying to catch up, and it means the budget you agreed in January is the one thing in your company that has not changed.

Adriana, a small thing but a useful one. This morning at breakfast, before the meeting started, the chief financial officer asked me what I thought about the shipping story, and I froze. Not because I did not have an opinion, but because I did not have it in English. Three people were listening. It lasted ten seconds and it was the longest ten seconds of my week. So here is my advice, and it is not about grammar. Read one business story a day, in English, and prepare two sentences about it. Not five. Two. One that says what happened, and one that says what it means for us. That is the whole conversation, and it is the one that people remember you by.
